question: For the paper "A Short Review of Ethical Challenges in Clinical Natural Language Processing" (arXiv: 1703.10090), answer this question: What sources of less sensitive data are available?

assessment.supported_part: The paper identifies sources of less sensitive data: (1) derived data, i.e., text fragments, various statistics and trained models that cannot reconstruct the original text or re-identify individuals, and (2) surrogate data, i.e., health-related texts from social media and patient-generated data available online.

Data that can not be used to reconstruct the original text (and when sanitized, can not directly re-identify the individual) include text fragments, various statistics and trained mod- els.

Next, the work on surrogate data has re- cently seen a surge in activity. Increasingly more health-related texts are produced in social media (Abbasi et al., 2014), and patient-generated data are available online.

passages.text: How- ever, this potential has remained largely untapped due to slow progress primarily caused by strict data access policies for re- searchers. In this paper, we discuss the concern for privacy and the measures it entails. We also suggest sources of less sensitive data. Finally, we draw attention to biases that can compromise the validity of empirical research and lead to socially harmful applications.

Another way of reducing sensitivity of data and improving chances for IRB approval is to work on derived data. Data that can not be used to reconstruct the original text (and when sanitized, can not directly re-identify the individual) include text fragments, various statistics and trained mod- els.

passages.title: A Short Review of Ethical Challenges in Clinical Natural Language Processing
passages.text: It is not entirely clear though how often this possibility has been used in clinical NLP research or broader. Next, the work on surrogate data has re- cently seen a surge in activity. Increasingly more health-related texts are produced in social media (Abbasi et al., 2014), and patient-generated data are available online. Admittedly, these may not resemble the clinical discourse, yet they bear to the same individuals whose health is documented in the clinical reports.

passages.title: A Short Review of Ethical Challenges in Clinical Natural Language Processing
passages.text: Dual use We have already mentioned linking personal health information from online texts to clinical records as a motivation for exploring sur- rogate data sources. However, this and many other applications also have potential to be applied in both beneﬁcial and harmful ways. It is easy to imagine how sensitive information from clinical notes can be revealed about an individual who is present in social media with a known identity.

passages.text: San- itization of sensitive data categories and individu- als’ informed consent are in the forefront of those legislative acts and bear immediate consequences for the NLP research. The GDPR lists general principles relating to processing of personal data, including that pro- cessing must be lawful (e.g. by means of con- sent), fair and transparent; it must be done for ex- plicit and legitimate purposes; and the data should be kept limited to what is necessary and as long as necessary.
